Morey 2005 (standing in for the listed 2008 chapter, which condenses it) adds: Aiton is tonal (3 tones), unstressed syllables exist (schwa reduction in function words and presyllables), and no word-stress placement rule is given because prosodic analysis was not undertaken. new_statements.rule_in_words: Aiton is a tone language (three contrastive tones in contemporary Aiton per Morey's Table 6.68, with tones 4 and 5 as allotones). The book gives no rule for the placement of word stress; it only notes that some syllables are 'unstressed' (unstressed function words and the presyllable of sesquisyllabic words like sa¹ rā¹ 'Buddhist monk', where the vowel reduces to schwa) and states explicitly that prosodic (stress/intonation) analysis of the Tai languages of Northeast India 'has not been possible and remains an area for further research'. By implication prominence falls on full-tone syllables, i.e. on the final (main) syllable of sesquisyllables, but Morey does not state a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tone-related: tone 4 (mid rising) is a sporadic allotone of tone 1; tone 5 (stopped) only on checked syllables; in Phake/Khamti polysyllabic Pali loans the unstressed middle syllable takes the level 1st tone, raising the question of toneless syllables (p.133, said of Phake/Khamti, not Aiton).
new_statements.identity_note: Morey 2005 describes the Aiton of the Aiton villages of Karbi Anglong and Golaghat districts, Assam (informants Bidya Thoumoung, Sa Cham Thoumoung, Nabin Shyam Phalung, Sui Khong Thoumoung), alongside Phake, Khamyang and Khamti; the Aiton-specific phonology is §6.3 (pp.140-170). Statements quoted from §4.2.1 (p.81) cover all the Tai languages of Northeast India; the p.133 remark on toneless/unstressed loan syllables concerns Phake and Khamti, not Aiton.

tone_statements.quote: In preliminary discussions with Bidya Thoumoung and other Aiton informants in November 1999, five tones were recognised. ... After putting together Table 6.67, a word list of about 2000 items was elicited from Bidya Thoumoung and recorded. He was then asked to indicate which tone each word had. While working through the word list, it became clear that Bidya Thoumoung assigned Tone [5] only to dead or checked syllables, and Tone [3] only to syllables with final nasals or final vowels, and that therefore Tones [3 and 5] were probably allotones of the same toneme. Tone [4] was rarely assigned ... It therefore appeared that tone [4] was a sporadic allotone of Tone 1. On the basis of this, the following tone box is proposed for contemporary Aiton (Table 6.68): ... 1. mid/high level, mid rising; 2. high level then falling; 3. mid falling glottalised, mid falling. Examples of the three tones are given in Table 6.69

For the latter varieties, tones have been numbered to accord with Harris's Khamti insofar as systems agree. [Table 2. Tonal Systems: Aiton1 A: H 3rs, M-G 1hfl, L 1hfl; B: H 3rs, M-G 3rs, L 1hfl; C: 2mfl, 2mfl, 2mfl; D: H 3m/h, M-G 3m/h, L 1l. Aiton2 A: H 4lrs, M-G 3hfl, L 3hfl; B: H 6mrs, M-G 6mrs, L 1l; C: H 5mflq, M-G 5mflq, L 2mfl; D: H 6m/h, M-G 6m/h, L 1l. Abbreviations: h - high, m - mid, l - low, rs - rising, fl - falling (unspecified contour indicates relatively level), q - relatively salient constriction and/or creak and/or final glottal stop] ... The three-tone system of Aiton1 can be seen as a compression of the fuller and undoubtedly more conservative system Aiton2, which in turn is rather similar to Phake. Among the merged distinctions in Aiton1 is the falling together of C-category items distinguished on the basis of a "laryngeal component" in Aiton2 and Phake.

audit.reasoning: The record codes Aiton as 'tonal' with no word-stress rule, resting on Morey 2005, the Pacific Linguistics reference grammar by the language's principal describer; both the deciding tone passage (pp. 161-162) and the domain/vowel-reduction passage (p. 155) are verbatim in the held archive.org text. Glottolog has only one descriptive ref (a 2018 Tezpur masters thesis), so nothing outranks Morey. I downloaded and scanned Morey's 2005 LTBA article (open, SEAlang), whose Aiton section (pp. 162-165) independently confirms the three-tone analysis and uses 'stressed' only for phrase-level prominence conditioning a rising allotone of Tone 1; Morey 2014 (LD&C, open) is Phake-centred and silent on Aiton stress; Borah 2020 (Shodhganga, Assamese) could not be read. No source seen suggests a word-stress system; works still to obtain are low priority corroboration only.

sources.note: Per Morey 2005 sect. 3.2.16.1 (pp.58-59) and 6.3.4.1.1.1 (pp.157-158): Banchob (1977) 'listed seven tones which she identified for Aiton' - 1 high, 2 high with final falling, 3 low with final rising, 4 falling, 5 low, 6 rising, 7 falling with a high onset; Morey derives a Gedney tone box from her word list (Table 6.62) and notes she 'was never satisfied with her analysis of the Aiton tones' and that it is inconsistent with her dictionary MS. First-hand 1970s notation, i.e. an earlier and richer tone inventory than the 3-tone system listed here.

sources.note: Per Morey 2005 sect. 6.3.4.1.1.2 (pp.158-159): 'In the Aiton-English-Thai Dictionary, Banchob notates ten tones, but most of them are very infrequently used. Only tones 1, 2, 8, 9 & 10 are used widely'; Morey shows tones 1/8/10 are one toneme and that 'with very few exceptions, a three tone system can be posited for the Aiton recorded in Banchob's Aiton-English-Thai Dictionary'. Tone-marked lexicon, first-hand.
